units: a covered market is in poor condition
the roof lets water through
the sellers are short of space
the aisles are crowded with shoppers
inspectors have declared the place unhealthy
a group of sellers puts forward a three-part answer
the requests concern the roof, the aisles and the drainage
a local body has approved the idea but lacks money
the work would be done in the slow season
the sellers hope the buyers will come back
text: The market hall down in the lower streets no longer keeps anything dry. Its timber frame is rotting, broken panes let the rain straight in, and the concrete floor turns slick the moment the damp rises. Sellers complain of cramped stalls that press against one another, while shoppers shuffle along an aisle packed shoulder to shoulder. A traders' group has put forward an answer in three parts. They want the roof rebuilt first, then the central walkways widened, and finally a drainage system laid in, since inspectors have called the building unfit and unhealthy. The district council backs the idea and is still hunting for the money. Work would begin in the slow season, so that no stall has to shut. The traders will put up with the mess, sure that a repaired hall will win back the buyers who had been drifting away.

units: two public spaces are set side by side
one is old and the other recent
trees surround the older one
you can stay there without spending
the new space is bright but has no shade
the noise puts off anyone who would like to stay
the old one was designed for pausing and the recent one for moving through
the writer holds that a place is judged by those who stay in it for no reason
text: People like to set the old square against the recent forecourt, as though one belonged to the past and the other to what comes next. The contrast is worth a closer look. The old square, ringed by close-planted trees, invites you to sit down without buying anything: an idle old man, children at a run, a stallholder dozing in the warmth. The recent forecourt gleams with pale paving and hard-edged benches, yet it throws no shade at all, and its clatter drives off anyone who might want to linger. One was drawn for the quiet halt, the other for passing through. We are too quick to judge a shared space by how it shines. It should be judged by how many people stay in it for no reason. A place that works is not one you cross. It is one you inhabit for a moment, then leave with regret.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a mediator works in a defined district
her work falls into four parts
she handles disputes between neighbors
she receives both sides in a neutral place
she helps people with official paperwork
she runs meetings and trains volunteers
she records closed cases with great care
her colleagues praise her warmth and her helpfulness
she studied social law before taking the post
text: Four strands make up the work of the mediator assigned to the northern district, each of them set out in a written protocol. The first covers quarrels between neighbors: she takes in the complaint, checks whether it can be handled, and then calls both sides into a neutral room. The second deals with rights and entitlements, so she helps people fill in forms and points them toward the office that can rule on it. The third is prevention, since she runs meetings in the housing blocks and trains the volunteers who will go on to lead them. The fourth is record-keeping, and here she is exacting, because every closed case has to be coded. Colleagues describe her as warm with the public and quick to help newer staff. She studied social law before taking the post, and added a course in active listening.

units: a redevelopment scheme is assessed phase by phase
the consultation of residents was serious
the documents and the objections were made public
an option preserving a courtyard was rejected without explanation
the work went ahead quickly
the signage hindered the oldest residents
the finished result looks solid and clear
the final judgment is mixed
the writer hopes the early method will be used again elsewhere
text: Following this redevelopment scheme stage by stage is the surest way to weigh what it achieved. The opening phase, an open consultation with residents, was handled with real rigor: minutes were circulated, objections recorded, deadlines met. The second stage disappoints, because the client dropped the option that would have preserved the inner courtyard and gave no adequate reason for doing so. Construction followed, carried out at a speed that deserves credit, though the signage badly confused the older residents. Handover, at last, reveals a plain ensemble whose materials look durable and whose walkways read clearly. The verdict is therefore divided: an exemplary method at the start, an opaque ruling in the middle, a respectable outcome. One would like the next scheme to keep the first of those qualities without repeating the second failing.

units: the writer has just moved somewhere else
the building looked in good condition in the pictures
the shared areas turned out to be damaged
the lack of upkeep had discouraged the occupants
that discouragement made the decay worse
the writer called a meeting between neighbors
few people came for lack of information
those present shared out the cleaning and wrote to the landlord
the state of the building has improved since
the writer asks for news from the person addressed
text: I am writing to you from the place I have just moved into, and I think you will see straight away where my head is. The building looked perfectly sound in the photographs I was shown. When I got here I found a battered stairwell, mailboxes that had been pried open, and an entry phone that made no sound at all. Since nobody was looking after the shared areas, the neighbors had given up trying, and that giving up let the damage spread further. So I called a meeting. Word never really got round, so few people came, but we were enough to settle on two things. We split the cleaning floor by floor, and we wrote to the landlord together. Since then the stairs are lit, the front door shuts properly, and the neighbors say hello on the stairs. Now tell me how your own move went, because I would like to hold it up against mine.

units: vehicles take up the sidewalk of the street
people have to walk in the lane used by cars
the writer holds that action is possible without waiting for the authorities
the residents logged the blocked crossings for a week
they took pictures and wrote a short document
a local committee must give an opinion on a car-free scheme
two bollards were put in at a street corner
the roads department promised to paint markings
the writer sums up the method in three moves
text: You asked me what has gone wrong on our street, so here it is, straight. The trouble is that the whole width of the sidewalk gets used as parking, which means we walk in the roadway with the strollers. The next question answers itself: can we do anything without waiting for some ruling from above? We can, and we started. For a week we logged every blocked crossing, we took pictures, we put together a short note. Then you will say: who ever reads a note like that? The district committee does, as it happens, because it has to give an opinion before the plan for a street without cars goes forward. The upshot is two bollards on the corner and a promise from the roads department to paint markings. It has not worked everywhere, granted, but the method holds: watch, count, ask in writing.

units: a volunteer compares two districts outside a community center
in the lower district people come in person
in the upper district they phone instead of travelling
the manager puts the gap down to distance
a woman using the service describes a packed waiting room below
the matching room above is almost empty
the number of staff differs between the two places
the volunteer finds the comparison incomplete without that fact
the speakers agree on the part played by available staff
text: Asked for her view outside the community center, a volunteer weighs up the two districts she knows. Down here, she says, people knock on the door when they need a form; up the hill they phone first and rarely make the trip in person. The manager softens that: the gap comes from distance, he argues, not from any difference in the people. An older woman using the service cuts in to say the waiting room down here is packed from opening time, while the one up the hill struck her as nearly empty. The manager grants the difference and puts it down to staffing, two workers below and one above. The volunteer concludes that the comparison would be unfair if that detail were left out. All three settle on the same point: what gets done depends less on the district than on how many hands are free.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: farming communities managed their own water
this management covered several aspects
the upkeep of the water point fell to every household
the basin was cleaned and the leaks checked
the sharing followed an order of turns that was respected
that order decided whether the crops did well
a gathering of elders punished those who broke the rule
the punishment was the loss of a watering turn
these rules were handed down by word of mouth
they lasted as long as the mutual dependence did
text: Long before water ran from a tap, farming communities took charge of it themselves, and that work fell into several separate parts. There was the spring first of all, kept up by every household: the basin was scoured, the loose stones reset, the seepage watched closely. There was the sharing next, governed by turns that nobody dared jump, since the order of watering decided how the crops came in. And there was punishment, handed down by a gathering of elders who stripped the offending household of its next turn. None of these rules were ever set down in writing. They passed from one mouth to another, held in the use and the memory of neighbors. What strikes you, looking back from a distance, is how long they lasted, as long as the mutual dependence that had brought them into being.

units: a shared budget runs through ordered stages
residents first put in their proposals
every proposal follows the same form
technical staff then judge what can be built
requests that cost too much or fall outside the scope are dropped
the proposals kept are costed and then grouped by area
the vote is held at reception points spread around
the highest placed projects enter the works program
progress is made public at regular intervals
the procedure runs again from one year to the next
text: A scheme for a shared budget runs through a fixed sequence, and it is easy to set out step by step. It opens with a call for ideas, so any resident writes a proposal on a standard form, with a short description and the place it would apply to. Technical staff then look at whether each submission can actually be built, and they throw out whatever belongs to another budget or goes past the ceiling that was set. Next comes the appraisal stage, where the surviving proposals are costed and then grouped by area. Voting follows, over a short window, at reception points spread across the territory. The proposals that come out on top are written into the works program, and a progress table is published at every stage. The whole calendar repeats from one year to the next with no real change.

units: an elevator broke down in a building
two occupants were stuck between two floors
one of them was elderly and the other very young
the repair was slow in coming
neighbors spoke to them and brought them something to drink
one resident kept phoning the firm in charge
the two occupants were freed during the night
the residents then drew up an internal contact list
they called for stricter servicing
the manager agreed to replace the worn cables
text: It took nothing more than a broken elevator for the building to discover something about itself. The car came to a halt between two floors on an evening of driving rain, with an elderly resident and a teenager shut inside. No repair crew came quickly, so the wait stretched on and on, and word of it travelled from landing to landing. One neighbor went down to talk through the door, another brought a bottle of water, a third kept phoning the firm that held the contract. The consequence was not only that the two were freed, late into the night. Because they had finally spoken to one another, the residents drew up a list of contacts the following week, and then they demanded that the servicing be carried out far more strictly. The manager, named in writing, agreed to replace the worn cables.
